lesson.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

steps.headline: Cells transfer energy from fuel into ATP, then spend ATP on their work.

lead.text: Respiration is a set of chemical reactions that transfer energy from fuel such as glucose.
Much of that energy goes into ATP, a small molecule that cells spend on work. The rest disperses as heat. Using oxygen is called aerobic respiration.
Plants make sugar only when there is light. Yet they are alive around the clock, and living cells always have work to do.

reveal.text: You named the process that runs on stored fuel. It needs no light, so it carries on in the dark.

steps.headline: Complete aerobic oxidation of three glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Three glucose hold three lots of six.
Each carbon atom ends up in one CO₂, so there are 18.

steps.headline: Complete aerobic oxidation of two glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?

workedSteps.text: One glucose holds six carbon atoms.
Each carbon atom ends up in one CO₂.

steps.headline: Breathing moves air. Cellular respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

lead.text: Breathing brings oxygen in and carries carbon dioxide out. Cellular respiration is what happens inside cells: reactions that use that oxygen and the fuel.
The two are linked, but they are different things.
Respiring organisms in a sealed jar use oxygen, so the oxygen amount falls. Measure it at the start and again later.

reveal.text: You measured respiration by the oxygen that disappeared. The same method works for any living material in a sealed jar.

lead.text: Careful experimenters also set up a blank: an identical jar with no organisms. It shows what the apparatus does by itself.

reveal.text: The blank separated the organisms' use from the apparatus's. Without it, the whole drop would have been credited to the organisms.

lesson.orientation: Connect respiration, ATP and conserved atoms without confusing breathing with cellular reactions.
lesson.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A candle burns wax with oxygen. It gives out heat, light, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Your cells treat sugar in a similar way, without any flame.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how a cell transfers energy from fuel and follow its carbon atoms, and tell breathing from respiration.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why you need food and oxygen, and why you breathe out carbon dioxide.

recap.keyIdea: Respiration transfers energy from fuel into ATP, and conserves the fuel's atoms in its products. Breathing is not the same thing.

blocks.text: You counted the CO₂ that two and then three glucose molecules produce.
You also measured oxygen use in a sealed jar and removed the blank's loss from the total.

recap.nextHook: Cells must copy their DNA before they divide. How does a cell copy a message one base at a time?

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: The name is three letters long.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.onCorrect: ATP. Cells fill it with energy from fuel, then spend it on work.

misconceptions.feedback: Glucose is the fuel. Name the molecule that carries the transferred energy to the work.

questions.prompt: Complete aerobic oxidation of two glucose molecules produces how many CO₂ molecules?
hints: Count the carbon from two glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each carbon atom from the fuel ends up in one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the CO₂ from one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. It runs on stored fuel, so it carries on when the light goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Photosynthesis needs light, and there is none. Name the process that uses fuel.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of living organisms holds 20 units of oxygen at the start and 11 units after three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the starting and final oxygen amounts.
Subtract the final amount from the starting amount.
questions.onCorrect: 9 units. Falling oxygen in a sealed jar is a sign that organisms are respiring.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was left. The question asks how much was used.
That adds the two amounts. Oxygen fell, so subtract.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon during complete aerobic oxidation?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

questions.onCorrect: It ends up in carbon dioxide. Atoms are conserved, and only the energy is transferred.

misconceptions.feedback: Matter doesn't turn into energy. The carbon atoms are still there afterwards.
Oxygen gas has no carbon in it. Look for a product that does.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: Compare moving air with cellular chemistry.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing can supply oxygen, but respiration is a set of chemical processes in cells.

choices.label: They are exactly the same reaction
Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air. Respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is a movement of air, not a reaction. Respiration is the reaction.
Plants and bacteria respire too, and they do not breathe.

questions.prompt: Not all the energy from fuel ends up in ATP. In what form does much of the rest disperse?
hints: Think about why your body is warm.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy that is not transferred to ATP disperses as heat.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Some energy always disperses as heat, which is why living things are warm.

misconceptions.feedback: Most cells give out very little light. Think about what a warm body gives off.

questions.prompt: A cell completely oxidises five glucose molecules. How many carbon atoms end up in CO₂?
hints: How many carbon atoms does one glucose have?
All the carbon from the fuel ends up in CO₂.
Multiply the carbon atoms in one glucose by five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and all of them end up in CO₂: 5 × 6 = 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. Carbon is conserved, so every carbon atom in the fuel ends up in CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon in one glucose. There are five.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: Which gas do you breathe out that comes from this process?
hints: It is also what a candle gives out.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cells release carbon dioxide when they use sugar as fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Cells use sugar and oxygen, and carbon dioxide is one of the products.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is what the cells use up. Name the gas they give out.

questions.prompt: Why can you count the CO₂ by counting the carbon atoms in the fuel?
hints: Think about what happens to atoms in any chemical reaction.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms are conserved, so the carbon from the fuel ends up in the products.

choices.label: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
Carbon atoms are turned into energy

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are conserved. The carbon is rearranged into CO₂, so the counts match.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy and atoms are different things. Atoms are never turned into energy in a cell.
Oxygen is a reactant here, but the carbon comes from the fuel.

questions.prompt: A blank jar with no organisms also loses 2 units of oxygen in the same three minutes, while the organism jar loses 9. How many units did the organisms themselves use?
hints: Some oxygen is lost even without organisms.
The blank shows the loss that is not the organisms' doing.
Take the blank's loss off the organisms' jar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 units. The blank's loss is not the organisms' doing.

questions.onCorrect: 7 units. The blank shows the loss due to the apparatus, so subtract it to isolate the organisms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the organism jar's total loss. Part of it also happens in the blank.
That adds the two losses. The blank's loss should come off.
